intro: Olive oil ice cream is not a health food. It is a Mediterranean dessert technique, where extra virgin olive oil is churned into the base for a silkier texture and a fruity, peppery note plain cream cannot give.
This covers how the oil goes in, why a good extra virgin's character comes through more than in a neutral-oil dessert, a simple finish, and a no-churn version for a reader without a machine.

sections.heading: A churned dessert, not a health swap

blocks.text: Olive oil ice cream sits in the same family as gelato made with milk instead of heavy cream: a technique aimed at texture and flavour, not a lighter or better-for-you version of the classic. Whether it suits any particular diet is a question for a doctor or dietitian, not this article.
The oil changes mouthfeel and taste. Fat coats the tongue and slows how fast ice crystals melt, and extra virgin olive oil brings its own fruitiness along, in a way a neutral oil never would.

sections.heading: How the oil goes into the base

blocks.text: The oil joins the cream in a custard base or replaces part of it, then gets emulsified in while the machine churns, rather than poured in at the end. A slow, steady stream into the still-cold, moving base is what keeps it from separating.

sections.heading: Why extra virgin's fruit and pepper come through

blocks.text: A neutral oil disappears into a dessert and leaves only richness behind. Extra virgin olive oil keeps its own identity: a grassy or fruity front note and a peppery catch at the back of the throat, both of which survive churning and cold far better than they survive baking heat.

That peppery edge cuts the sweetness, the way a squeeze of lemon might on a savoury dish. A milder extra virgin sits politely alongside vanilla or citrus; a sharper one suits a plainer base that lets it lead.

The base rarely needs more than one finishing touch once scooped: flaky salt for a savoury-sweet contrast, or fresh orange or lemon zest for a brighter top note that echoes the oil's own fruitiness. A last thread of oil drizzled over the scoop repeats the flavour rather than introducing a new one.

items: **Flaky salt** — a small pinch scattered just before serving.
**Citrus zest** — orange or lemon, grated over the scoop for a fruitier oil.
**A final thread of oil** — a few drops on top, for a stronger finish.

blocks.text: Whipped cream folded with sweetened condensed milk and olive oil sets in the freezer without any churning at all, and skips the custard step entirely. The texture is a touch denser than a churned base, but the same oil, salt and zest choices still apply.

items: Whip 400 ml chilled heavy cream to soft peaks.
Whisk 200 ml condensed milk with 80 ml olive oil and a pinch of salt.
Fold the condensed-milk mixture into the cream, in three additions.
Pour into a lidded container and smooth the top.
Freeze at least six hours before scooping.

blocks.text: A milder extra virgin suits a vanilla or citrus base, and a sharper, peppery one suits a plainer base built to let the oil lead. Either way, use the plain extra virgin — see [the products page](products) — not one of the infused flavours.

faqs.q: Is olive oil ice cream healthier than regular ice cream?
faqs.a: That is a question for a doctor or dietitian, not a recipe guide. This article covers the technique only: how the oil goes into the base, and what it does to texture.

faqs.q: Does olive oil ice cream taste like olive oil?
faqs.a: It tastes faintly of the fruit the oil was pressed from — grassy or peppery depending on the oil — as a counter-note to the sweetness, not as the dominant flavour once the base is churned and frozen.

faqs.q: Can I make olive oil ice cream without a machine?
faqs.a: Yes. Whip cream to soft peaks, fold in sweetened condensed milk mixed with olive oil and a pinch of salt, then freeze in a lidded container for at least six hours before scooping.

faqs.q: How much olive oil goes into an ice cream base?
faqs.a: Roughly 80 to 100 ml of extra virgin olive oil against 750 ml of combined milk and cream is a workable starting ratio, streamed in slowly while the base is churning rather than stirred in cold.

faqs.q: Which olive oil suits ice cream best?
faqs.a: A milder, fruitier extra virgin suits a vanilla or citrus base; a sharper, peppery one suits a plainer base built to let the oil lead. Either way, use the plain extra virgin, not an infused flavour.

faqs.q: Why does the oil need to be added while churning?
faqs.a: A slow stream into a cold, moving base is what keeps the oil emulsified rather than floating free. Poured in cold at the end, it tends to separate instead of blending into the texture.

faqs.q: What can I add on top of olive oil ice cream?
faqs.a: Flaky salt or fresh orange or lemon zest, scattered on just before serving, both echo the oil's own fruitiness. A final thread of the same oil over the scoop repeats the flavour rather than adding a new one.
